data.description: Drainage systems for excess body fluids and associated methods are disclosed herein. A body fluid drainage system in accordance with an embodiment of the present technology, for example, can include a catheter that has an exterior surface, a proximal portion, and a distal portion opposite the proximal portion. The body fluid drainage system can further include a valve device, a pressure sensor, and a controller operatively coupled to the valve device and the pressure sensor. The valve device can include an actuator positioned over the exterior surface of the catheter. The actuator is movable between an open position that allows body fluid flow through the catheter, a closed position that at least substantially obstructs the body fluid flow through the catheter, and intermediate positions that partially obstruct the body fluid flow through the catheter. The controller can change the position of the actuator in response to a predetermined condition of the pressure sensor.

  <section>
    <h2>Definitions</h2>
    <ul>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the present technology</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">relates generally to draining excess body fluids.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0002">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">several embodiments</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">are directed toward body fluid drainage systems with enhanced drainage regulation and associated methods.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0002">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">Hydrocephalus</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">for example, is an accumulation of excess cerebrospinal fluid (“CSF”) in the ventricles of the brain that increases intracranial pressure (“ICP”). This condition can be caused by the inability to reabsorb CSF, impaired CSF flow, or excessive production of CSF. Acute accumulations of excess CSF can also occur from brain trauma, brain hemorrhaging, strokes, brain tumors, spinal fluid leaks, meningitis, and brain abscesses. When left untreated, hydrocephalus and other excess accumulations of CSF can progressively enlarge the ventricles of the brain, which can increase ICP and cause convulsions, mental disabilities, and eventually death.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0003">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">CSF</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">cerebrospinal fluid</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0003">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">ICP</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">intracranial pressure</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0003">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">a ventriculoperitoneal shunt</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">(“VPS”), for example, includes a subcutaneously installed catheter inserted in the lateral ventricle (i.e., a site of excess CSF) and in fluid communication with the peritoneal cavity to facilitate reabsorbtion of the excess CSF into the body.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0004">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">a mechanical valve</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">generally implanted flush with the skull, can regulate CSF flow through the catheter.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0004">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">VPSs</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can regulate CSF movement based on static pressure parameters. For example, an external magnetic field can be applied to the implanted VPS to change the set point pressure of the valve.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0004">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">temporary CSF diversion</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">generally includes the installation of an external ventricular drain (“EVD”) that funnels CSF from the lateral ventricle to an external drainage chamber, and thereby reduces the intracranial CSF volume and lowers ICP.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0005">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">EVD</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">external ventricular drain</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0005">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">temporary CSF diversion</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can include placing a lumbar drain (“LD”) at the base of the spine, and draining CSF from the lumbar region to an external drainage chamber.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0005">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">LD</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">lumbar drain</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0005">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">EVDs and LDs</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">use the similar components to control drainage.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0005">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">VPSs</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">temporary and more permanent CSF diversion devices</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0006">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">Infection</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">for example, can be a significant risk factor both during and after implantation of a CSF shunt.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0006">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the entire CSF shunt</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">must be removed, and the patient must generally undergo 10-14 days of IV antibiotics and re-internalization of a new CSF shunt.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0006">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">Mechanical failure</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can occur within each component of a CSF shunt, and generally requires the replacement of the failed component(s).</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0006">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the inlet of the catheter</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">for example, can incur in-growth of intraventricular tissue.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0006">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">Valves</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can fail due to debris build-up (e.g., blood, protein) within the valve, and the outlet of the catheter can fail by fracturing, becoming obstructed, or tethering within scar tissue.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0006">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">debris build-up</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">e.g., blood, protein</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0006">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">fracturing</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">e.g., blood, protein</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0006">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">tethering</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">e.g., tethering within scar tissue.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0006">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 1A</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a schematic view of an internal body fluid drainage system installed within a patient in accordance with an embodiment of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0007">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 1B</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a schematic view of an external body fluid drainage system installed in a patient in accordance with an embodiment of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0008">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 2A</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is an enlarged schematic, cross-sectional view of a valve device in accordance with an embodiment of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0009">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 2B</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is an enlarged schematic, cross-sectional view of a valve device in accordance with another embodiment of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0010">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIGS. 3A-3J</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">are side views of actuators for a valve device in accordance with embodiments of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0011">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIGS. 4A and 4B</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">are side and perspective views, respectively, of reservoirs for a body fluid drainage system in accordance with embodiments of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0012">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 5A</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a schematic, cross-sectional top plan view of unobstructed antegrade flow through a valve device of a body fluid drainage system in accordance with an embodiment of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0013">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 5B</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a schematic, cross-sectional top plan view of partially obstructed antegrade flow through the valve device of FIG. 5A .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0014">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 5C</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a schematic, cross-sectional top plan view of retrograde flow through the valve device of FIG. 5A .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0015">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 5D</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a schematic, cross-sectional top plan view of forced antegrade flow through the valve device of FIG. 5A .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0016">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 6A</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a schematic, cross-sectional side view of antegrade flow through a body fluid drainage system implanted in a ventricle in accordance with an embodiment of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0017">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 6B</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a schematic, cross-sectional top view of retrograde flow through the body fluid drainage system of FIG. 6A .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0018">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 7A</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a partial schematic view of a body fluid drainage system in accordance with a further embodiment of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0019">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIGS. 7B-7D</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">are schematic views of portions of the body fluid drainage system of FIG. 7A .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0020">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIGS. 8A and 8B</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">are schematic views of external body fluid drainage systems installed in different portions of a CSF system in accordance with additional embodiments of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0021">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">a body fluid drainage system</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be installed between a site of excess body fluid in a patient and a second location (e.g., an external receptacle, an internal cavity) that can collect and/or reabsorb the excess body fluid.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0022">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the body fluid drainage system</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can include a valve device that applies incremental forces to an exterior of a catheter to regulate the drainage rate of the body fluid.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0022">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the body fluid drainage system</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can also generate forced flow of the body fluid through the catheter to both prevent obstructions and perform diagnostics on the system.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0022">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">CSF</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">cerebrospinal fluid</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0022">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">present technology</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">may be used to drain a variety of excess body fluids, such as peritoneal fluid, blood, water, and/or other body fluids.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0022">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">catheter</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is used broadly throughout the application to refer to any suitable tubing or structure that includes a lumen through which body fluids can flow.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0022">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">Other details describing well-known structures and systems often associated with CSF and other body fluid drainage systems, shunts, biomedical diagnostics, etc.</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">have not been set forth in the following disclosure to avoid unnecessarily obscuring the description of the various embodiments of the technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0022">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">a person of ordinary skill in the art</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">therefore, will accordingly understand that the technology may have other embodiments with additional elements, or the technology may have other embodiments without several of the features shown and described below with reference to FIGS. 1A-8B .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0022">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the term “force”</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">refers to the interaction between an actuator and a catheter. This term is used broadly, and in some embodiments “pressure” is an equally valid term. Additionally, in selected embodiments, the actuator can apply a force or a pressure to the catheter by changing the position of the actuator mechanism (e.g., a linear shaft, a rotary shaft, a screw shaft) relative to the catheter, thus “actuator position” may also be used to describe the interaction between the actuator and the catheter.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0023">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the actuator mechanism</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">e.g., a linear shaft, a rotary shaft, a screw shaft</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0023">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">FIG. 1A</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is a schematic view of an internal body fluid drainage system 100 (“drainage system 100 ”) implanted in a patient 101 in accordance with an embodiment of the present technology.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0024">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the drainage system 100</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can include a catheter 102 , a valve device 104 over an exterior surface 112 of the catheter 102 , and one or more sensors 106 (identified individually as a first sensor 106 a and a second sensor 106 b ).</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0024">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the drainage system 100</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can also include a controller 110 that is operatively coupled to the valve device 104 and/or the sensors 106 .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0024">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">valve device 104</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can apply incremental forces to the exterior surface 112 of the catheter 102 to regulate body fluid flow through the catheter 102 , and the controller 110 can alter the level of force applied by the valve device 104 on the catheter 102 in response to measurements (e.g., pressure, flow rate) taken from the sensors 106 .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0024">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">measurements</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">e.g., pressure, flow rate</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0024">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the catheter 102</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can include a proximal portion 108 a and a distal portion 108 b opposite the proximal portion 108 a .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0025">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the proximal and distal portions 108 a - b of the catheter 102</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be an integrally formed tube or include two or more separate tubes joined together using suitable fastening methods (e.g., gluing) known in the art.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0025">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the catheter 102</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be made from a range of polymers, such as silicone, latex, thermoplastic elastomers, and/or other suitable tubing materials.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0025">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">portions of the catheter proximate to the valve device 104</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can include compressible peristaltic pump tubing (e.g., silicone rubber, polyvinyl chloride), reduced fouling surfaces, tubing with different mechanical compliances, and/or other durable elastomeric materials that resist fatigue.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0025">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the catheter 102</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be made from tubing with biocides and/or other anti-biofouling agents that prevent organisms from entering the drainage system 100 and causing infection.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0025">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the catheter 102</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">includes different materials and/or sections of tubing, the different materials and/or portions can be sealed together with adhesives and/or other fasteners that provide a liquid-tight seal.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0025">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the proximal portion 108 a of the catheter 102</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is positioned at a site of excess body fluid and the distal portion 108 b can be placed in fluid communication with an internal receptacle that collects and/or absorbs the body fluid.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0026">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the proximal portion 108 a of the catheter 102</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can include an inlet region 116 with one or more openings (not visible) in fluid communication with a site of excess body fluid such that the body fluid can flow into the catheter 102 .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0026">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the inlet region 116 of the catheter 102</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">is installed (e.g., via a burr hole) into a ventricle 113 of the patient's brain to receive excess CSF.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0026">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the body fluid</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can travel in an antegrade flow through the catheter 102 to the distal portion 108 b .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0026">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the distal portion 108 b</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can include an outlet region 118 that expels the excess body fluid into an internal location.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0026">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the outlet region 118</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be placed in fluid communication with the patient's peritoneal cavity 115 , where excess body fluid can reabsorb into the body.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0026">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the outlet region 118</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can expel the body fluid into the atrium of the heart, the pleural lining of the lung, the gallbladder, and/or other suitable terminal locations.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0026">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the valve device 104</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be positioned between the proximal and distal portions 108 a - b of the catheter 102 to regulate the body fluid flow through the drainage system 100 .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0027">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the valve device 104</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be implanted in a subclavicular pocket of the patient 101 .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0027">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the valve device 104</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be installed in a prefascial or subfascial intra-abdominal region. This intra-abdominal positioning is particularly suited for neonates to ease exchange of the valve device 104 as the child grows, but also facilitates accessibility to the valve device 104 for adults.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0027">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">valve device 104</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">placement of the valve device 104 in either the subclavicular pocket or the intra-abdominal region negates the need to shave the patient's scalp to perform cranial surgery in the event that a component requires replacement or repair, and thus avoids the need for repeated incisions in the scalp that can cause devascularization, poor wound healing, and/or infection.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0027">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the intra-abdominal valve device 104</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">also eases the periodic replacement of batteries or other power sources.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0027">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the valve device 104</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be installed subcutaneously in other regions of the torso or between another site of excess body fluid and a receptacle that can collect and/or reabsorb the body fluid.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0027">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the valve device 104</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be miniaturized such that it can be implanted under the scalp.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0027">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the sensors 106</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can measure pressure within the catheter 102 , flow rate of the body fluid through the catheter 102 , and/or other desired measurements associated with body fluid drainage through the drainage system 100 .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0028">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">Pressure sensors</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be small electrical sensors positioned along the drainage device 100 .</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0028">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">Body fluid flow rate through the catheter 102</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be measured with a non-electrical Rotameter that uses a local or remote sensor to read the position of a weighted or buoyant ball that rises and falls within the catheter 102 in proportion to the flow rate.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0028">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">the body fluid flow rate</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">can be measured using what is known in the art as the “ice cube test.”</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0028">
      </li>
      <li itemprop="definitions" itemscope="" repeat="">
        <span itemprop="subject">An improved version of such a flow rate sensor</span>
        <span itemprop="definition">includes a resistive electrical heater and temperature sensor embedded in the body fluid flow, rather than an external heater/cooler and an external temperature measurement device used in conventional ice cube tests.</span>
        <meta itemprop="num_attr" content="0028">

  <section itemprop="abstract" itemscope="">
    <h2>Abstract</h2>
    
    <div itemprop="content" html=""><abstract mxw-id="PA195830265" lang="EN" load-source="patent-office">
    <div id="p-0001" num="0000" class="abstract">Drainage systems for excess body fluids and associated methods are disclosed herein. A body fluid drainage system in accordance with an embodiment of the present technology, for example, can include a catheter that has an exterior surface, a proximal portion, and a distal portion opposite the proximal portion. The body fluid drainage system can further include a valve device, a pressure sensor, and a controller operatively coupled to the valve device and the pressure sensor. The valve device can include an actuator positioned over the exterior surface of the catheter. The actuator is movable between an open position that allows body fluid flow through the catheter, a closed position that at least substantially obstructs the body fluid flow through the catheter, and intermediate positions that partially obstruct the body fluid flow through the catheter. The controller can change the position of the actuator in response to a predetermined condition of the pressure sensor.</div>
  </abstract>
  </div>
  </section>

  <section itemprop="description" itemscope="">
    <h2>Description</h2>
    
    <div itemprop="content" html=""><div mxw-id="PDES116101005" lang="EN" load-source="patent-office" class="description">
    
    <heading id="h-0001">CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATION(S)</heading>
    <div id="p-0002" num="0001" class="description-paragraph">This application claims the benefit of U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. 61/315,660, entitled “FAILURE RESISTANT SHUNT,” filed Mar. 19, 2010, and U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. 61/407,359, filed Oct. 27, 2010, entitled “EXTERNAL CSF DRAINAGE SYSTEM WITH IMPROVED VALVE AND OTHER FEATURES,” both of which are incorporated herein by reference in their entireties.</div>
    
    
    <heading id="h-0002">TECHNICAL FIELD</heading>
    <div id="p-0003" num="0002" class="description-paragraph">The present technology relates generally to draining excess body fluids. In particular, several embodiments are directed toward body fluid drainage systems with enhanced drainage regulation and associated methods.</div>
    <heading id="h-0003">BACKGROUND</heading>
    <div id="p-0004" num="0003" class="description-paragraph">A variety of medical conditions cause the collection of excess body fluids within the human body. Hydrocephalus, for example, is an accumulation of excess cerebrospinal fluid (“CSF”) in the ventricles of the brain that increases intracranial pressure (“ICP”). This condition can be caused by the inability to reabsorb CSF, impaired CSF flow, or excessive production of CSF. Acute accumulations of excess CSF can also occur from brain trauma, brain hemorrhaging, strokes, brain tumors, spinal fluid leaks, meningitis, and brain abscesses. When left untreated, hydrocephalus and other excess accumulations of CSF can progressively enlarge the ventricles of the brain, which can increase ICP and cause convulsions, mental disabilities, and eventually death.</div>
    <div id="p-0005" num="0004" class="description-paragraph">Treatment for hydrocephalus generally requires the installation of a CSF shunt that drains CSF from the brain to an alternate location that can collect the excess CSF or reabsorb it into the body. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt (“VPS”), for example, includes a subcutaneously installed catheter inserted in the lateral ventricle (i.e., a site of excess CSF) and in fluid communication with the peritoneal cavity to facilitate reabsorbtion of the excess CSF into the body. A mechanical valve, generally implanted flush with the skull, can regulate CSF flow through the catheter. Recent innovations have resulted in VPSs that can regulate CSF movement based on static pressure parameters. For example, an external magnetic field can be applied to the implanted VPS to change the set point pressure of the valve.</div>
    <div id="p-0006" num="0005" class="description-paragraph">Similar to hydrocephalus, acute accumulations of CSF are treated by shunting excess CSF to an alternate location. For example, temporary CSF diversion generally includes the installation of an external ventricular drain (“EVD”) that funnels CSF from the lateral ventricle to an external drainage chamber, and thereby reduces the intracranial CSF volume and lowers ICP. Alternatively, temporary CSF diversion can include placing a lumbar drain (“LD”) at the base of the spine, and draining CSF from the lumbar region to an external drainage chamber. Despite having different insertion points, EVDs and LDs use the similar components to control drainage.</div>
    <div id="p-0007" num="0006" class="description-paragraph">In general, temporary and more permanent CSF diversion devices (e.g., VPSs) include similar features, and thus incur many of the same complications. Infection, for example, can be a significant risk factor both during and after implantation of a CSF shunt. When an infection occurs, the entire CSF shunt must be removed, and the patient must generally undergo 10-14 days of IV antibiotics and re-internalization of a new CSF shunt. Mechanical failure can occur within each component of a CSF shunt, and generally requires the replacement of the failed component(s). The inlet of the catheter, for example, can incur in-growth of intraventricular tissue. Valves can fail due to debris build-up (e.g., blood, protein) within the valve, and the outlet of the catheter can fail by fracturing, becoming obstructed, or tethering within scar tissue. These mechanical failures, infections, and other complications cause a majority of implanted CSF shunts to fail within two years and nearly all shunts fail within ten years. Due to this unreliability and the necessity to locally monitor and adjust ICPs, conventional CSF shunts require frequent intervention by medical professionals.</div>

    <heading id="h-0005">DETAILED DESCRIPTION</heading>
    <div id="p-0023" num="0022" class="description-paragraph">The present technology is directed to devices, systems, and methods for draining excess body fluids. In one embodiment, for example, a body fluid drainage system can be installed between a site of excess body fluid in a patient and a second location (e.g., an external receptacle, an internal cavity) that can collect and/or reabsorb the excess body fluid. The body fluid drainage system can include a valve device that applies incremental forces to an exterior of a catheter to regulate the drainage rate of the body fluid. In selected embodiments, the body fluid drainage system can also generate forced flow of the body fluid through the catheter to both prevent obstructions and perform diagnostics on the system. Certain specific details are set forth in the following description and in <figref idrefs="DRAWINGS">FIGS. 1A-8B</figref> to provide a thorough understanding of various embodiments of the technology. For example, several embodiments of body fluid drainage systems that shunt cerebrospinal fluid (“CSF”) are described in detail below. The present technology, however, may be used to drain a variety of excess body fluids, such as peritoneal fluid, blood, water, and/or other body fluids. Additionally, the term “catheter” is used broadly throughout the application to refer to any suitable tubing or structure that includes a lumen through which body fluids can flow. Other details describing well-known structures and systems often associated with CSF and other body fluid drainage systems, shunts, biomedical diagnostics, etc. have not been set forth in the following disclosure to avoid unnecessarily obscuring the description of the various embodiments of the technology. A person of ordinary skill in the art, therefore, will accordingly understand that the technology may have other embodiments with additional elements, or the technology may have other embodiments without several of the features shown and described below with reference to <figref idrefs="DRAWINGS">FIGS. 1A-8B</figref>.</div>
    <div id="p-0024" num="0023" class="description-paragraph">As used herein, the term “force” refers to the interaction between an actuator and a catheter. This term is used broadly, and in some embodiments “pressure” is an equally valid term. Additionally, in selected embodiments, the actuator can apply a force or a pressure to the catheter by changing the position of the actuator mechanism (e.g., a linear shaft, a rotary shaft, a screw shaft) relative to the catheter, thus “actuator position” may also be used to describe the interaction between the actuator and the catheter.</div>

    <div id="p-0028" num="0027" class="description-paragraph">The <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> can be positioned between the proximal and distal portions <b>108</b> <i>a</i>-<i>b </i>of the <figure-callout id="102" label="catheter" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">catheter</a></figure-callout> <b>102</b> to regulate the body fluid flow through the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b>. This intra-abdominal positioning is particularly suited for neonates to ease exchange of the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> as the child grows, but also facilitates accessibility to the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> for adults.     <div id="p-0029" num="0028" class="description-paragraph">The sensors <b>106</b> can measure pressure within the <figure-callout id="102" label="catheter" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">catheter</a></figure-callout> <b>102</b>, flow rate of the body fluid through the <figure-callout id="102" label="catheter" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">catheter</a></figure-callout> <b>102</b>, and/or other desired measurements associated with body fluid drainage through the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b>. As shown in <figref idrefs="DRAWINGS">FIG. 1A</figref>, the sensors <b>106</b> can be positioned on either side of the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> to measure pressure upstream and downstream of the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b>. When the <figure-callout id="101" label="patient" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">patient</a></figure-callout> <b>101</b> is upright (i.e., standing), the <figure-callout id="106a" label="first sensor" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">first sensor</a></figure-callout> <b>106</b> <i>a </i>at the <figure-callout id="108a" label="proximal portion" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">proximal portion</a></figure-callout> <b>108</b> <i>a </i>can measure a pressure that is substantially equal to the ICP plus the pressure head created by the body fluid in the <figure-callout id="108a" label="proximal portion" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">proximal portion</a></figure-callout> <b>108</b> <i>a </i>above the <figure-callout id="106a" label="first sensor" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">first sensor</a></figure-callout> <b>106</b> <i>a</i>. The <figure-callout id="106b" label="second sensor" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">second sensor</a></figure-callout> <b>106</b> <i>b </i>at the <figure-callout id="108b" label="distal portion" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">distal portion</a></figure-callout> <b>108</b> <i>b </i>can measure a pressure substantially equal to the pressure at the outlet region <b>118</b> (e.g., the <figure-callout id="115" label="peritoneal cavity" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">peritoneal cavity</a></figure-callout> <b>115</b>; as is known in the art, the pressure is approximated as zero relative to atmosphere) plus the negative pressure created by the body fluid in the <figure-callout id="108b" label="distal portion" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">distal portion</a></figure-callout> <b>108</b> <i>b </i>below the <figure-callout id="106b" label="second sensor" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">second sensor</a></figure-callout> <b>106</b> <i>b</i>. The pressures from the upstream and downstream sensors <b>106</b> can be combined to derive the true ICP. For example, when the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> is positioned midway between the <figure-callout id="113" label="ventricle" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00002.png,US09662478-20170530-D00008.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">ventricle</a></figure-callout> <b>113</b> and the <figure-callout id="118" label="outlet region" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">outlet region</a></figure-callout> <b>118</b>, the summation of the two pressure measurements from the sensors <b>106</b> negates the contribution of pressure head and provides the true ICP.</div>
    <div id="p-0032" num="0031" class="description-paragraph">In other embodiments, as described in greater detail below with reference to <figref idrefs="DRAWINGS">FIGS. 7A-7D</figref>, a pressure reference line can be coupled to the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> and used to compensate for changes in patient position. The pressure reference line measures the pressure head between a desired reference location and the sensor <b>106</b> at the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> directly. As such, the desired pressure measurement (e.g., ICP) is simply the difference between the two measured pressures as taken from two independent sensors (i.e., the pressure reference line sensor and the drainage line sensor) or a single differential pressure sensor.</div>
    <div id="p-0033" num="0032" class="description-paragraph">The <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can also include an orientation sensor (not shown) to accurately measure a desired pressure (e.g., ICP) regardless of the orientation of the <figure-callout id="101" label="patient" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">patient</a></figure-callout> <b>101</b>. For example, the orientation sensor can include an accelerometer, inclinometer, and/or other orientation sensing device. The orientation sensor is used to determine the angle of repose (i.e., standing, lying, or therebetween); such that the measured angle and the known length of the <figure-callout id="108a" label="proximal portion" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">proximal portion</a></figure-callout> <b>108</b> <i>a </i>of the <figure-callout id="102" label="catheter" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">catheter</a></figure-callout> <b>102</b> can be used to calculate the pressure head. The pressure head can be subtracted from the measured pressure to calculate the true ICP.</div>
    <div id="p-0034" num="0033" class="description-paragraph">The <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b>, e.g., a microprocessor, can read the measurements taken from the sensors <b>106</b> (e.g., pressure, flow rate, orientation, etc.), store such measurements and other information in a database, adjust the position of the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b>, and/or carry out algorithms to regulate fluid flow through the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage device</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b>. For example, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can compare pressure measurements from the sensors <b>106</b> with a desired ICP to determine whether to incrementally open or close the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> and by what percentage. For example, when the pressure is lower than a desired pressure, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can incrementally close the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> to increase the resistance to antegrade flow through the <figure-callout id="102" label="catheter" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">catheter</a></figure-callout> <b>102</b>. If the sensed pressure is higher than desired, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can incrementally open the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> to decrease the resistance to antegrade flow. Similarly, the controller can also compare the sensed flow rate with a desired flow rate, and adjust the position of the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> accordingly. The <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can also carry out an algorithm that moves the valve device <b>104</b> a predetermined amount each time a measurement outside of a desired limit (e.g., desired CSF range) is detected. Such a control algorithm can also relate the incremental movement of the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> to the magnitude of the difference between a desired and a measured value. In other embodiments, a proportional-integral-derivative (“PID”) control algorithm or variations thereof (e.g., P-only, PI-only) can control the movement of the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b>. As such, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can manage body fluid flow in real-time to maintain the ICP and/or other desired parameter within appropriate limits across a range of changes in pressure or body fluid generation rate caused by physiologic processes (e.g., valsalva maneuvers, changes in body orientation).</div>
    <div id="p-0035" num="0034" class="description-paragraph">The <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can include algorithms that save power. For example, a tolerance window on the control parameter (e.g., ICP or CSF flow rate) can be defined such that the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> does not change position within the tolerance window. As another example, the time between sensor measurements can be adjusted based on the error between the desired set point and the measured value, such that less frequent measurements are made during periods of small error. These power-saving control algorithms can also be adapted to the dynamics of the specific application. During CSF drainage, for example, significant changes in CSF production may occur over several hours such that only infrequent sensor measurements and <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> movements are necessary for adequate flow control. As such, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can be configured to ignore unimportant transient conditions (e.g., ICP oscillations due to the cardiac cycle, ICP increases due to coughing or movement) removed by averaging sensor measurements and/or frequency filtering.</div>
    <div id="p-0036" num="0035" class="description-paragraph">Additionally, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can also include logic to clear the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> of obstructions by incrementally opening the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> until the obstruction clears. For example, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can be configured to maintain a desired ICP such that when an obstruction within the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> causes an increase in the measured pressure, the control algorithm (e.g., a proportional-integral-derivative) incrementally or fully opens the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> to decrease the resistance to antegrade flow. This incremental opening of the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> allows the obstruction to flow through the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> such that the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can maintain the desired ICP. As described in further detail below, in other embodiments, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can include logic that clears and/or prevents obstructions by flushing the <figure-callout id="102" label="catheter" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">catheter</a></figure-callout> <b>102</b> with body fluid.</div>
    <div id="p-0037" num="0036" class="description-paragraph">As further shown in <figref idrefs="DRAWINGS">FIG. 1A</figref>, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can include a time keeping device <b>124</b> (e.g., clock, timer, etc.) that is operatively coupled to the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b>. The <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can use the <figure-callout id="124" label="time keeping device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">time keeping device</a></figure-callout> <b>124</b> to sense pressure and/or flow rate at preset time intervals (e.g., once a minute). Additionally, as explained in further detail below, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can use the <figure-callout id="124" label="time keeping device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">time keeping device</a></figure-callout> <b>124</b> to periodically flush the <figure-callout id="102" label="catheter" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">catheter</a></figure-callout> <b>102</b> and/or periodically run diagnostics.</div>
    <div id="p-0038" num="0037" class="description-paragraph">Additionally, as shown in <figref idrefs="DRAWINGS">FIG. 1A</figref>, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can also include a <figure-callout id="122" label="power source" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">power source</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b> for the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> and/or other electrical features (e.g., the <figure-callout id="122" label="time keeping device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">time keeping device</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b>, the sensors <b>106</b>, etc.). The <figure-callout id="122" label="power source" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">power source</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b> can be stored locally within the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b>. As such, the <figure-callout id="122" label="power source" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">power source</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b> can thus include a lithium-ion cell, a rechargeable battery, and/or other suitable portable power sources. In selected embodiments, the internally installed <figure-callout id="122" label="power source" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">power source</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b> can be recharged remotely using inductive coupling, kinetic energy generation by M2E of Boise, Id., and/or other remote recharging methods known in the art. In other embodiments, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can connect to an external recharging station.</div>
    <div id="p-0039" num="0038" class="description-paragraph">In selected embodiments, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can be operatively coupled to a <figure-callout id="126" label="wireless communication link" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">wireless communication link</a></figure-callout> <b>126</b>, such as a WiFi connection, radio signal, and/or other suitable communication links that can send and/or receive information. The <figure-callout id="126" label="wireless communication link" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">wireless communication link</a></figure-callout> <b>126</b> allows measurements from the sensors <b>106</b> and/or other information to be monitored and/or analyzed remotely. For example, the <figure-callout id="126" label="wireless communication link" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">wireless communication link</a></figure-callout> <b>126</b> allows measurements recorded from the sensors <b>106</b> to be accessed at a doctor's office, at home by the <figure-callout id="101" label="patient" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">patient</a></figure-callout> <b>101</b>, and/or at other remote locations. Additionally, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can use the <figure-callout id="126" label="wireless communication link" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">wireless communication link</a></figure-callout> <b>126</b> to receive information at a WiFi hot spot or other remotely accessible locations. This allows a remote physician to inquiry the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> regarding particular measurements (e.g., ICP), instruct the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> to adjust the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> accordingly, and/or program sophisticated algorithms onto the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> for the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> to carry out. Accordingly, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can provide more expedient, sophisticated, and personalized treatment than conventional CSF shunts, without requiring frequent in-office visits.</div>
    <div id="p-0040" num="0039" class="description-paragraph">As further shown in <figref idrefs="DRAWINGS">FIG. 1A</figref>, the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b>, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b>, and/or other subcutaneously implanted features of the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can be enclosed within a <figure-callout id="128" label="housing" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">housing</a></figure-callout> <b>128</b>. Accordingly, the <figure-callout id="128" label="housing" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">housing</a></figure-callout> <b>128</b> can be made from a biocompatible material that protects the devices stored within from tissue ingrowth, body fluids, and/or other internal bodily features that may interfere with the operability of the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b>. In selected embodiments, the <figure-callout id="128" label="housing" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">housing</a></figure-callout> <b>128</b> can also form a magnetic shield over the devices within it such that the <figure-callout id="101" label="patient" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">patient</a></figure-callout> <b>101</b> can undergo magnetic resonance imaging (“MRI”) and similar procedures without removing the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b>.</div>
    <div id="p-0041" num="0040" class="description-paragraph">In operation, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can have generally low power consumption. For example, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> requires minimal, if any, continuous power. In one embodiment, the <figure-callout id="124" label="time keeping device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">time keeping device</a></figure-callout> <b>124</b> is the only feature of the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> that continuously draws from the <figure-callout id="122" label="power source" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">power source</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b>. Other devices can draw from the <figure-callout id="122" label="power source" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">power source</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b> intermittently as needed. For example, the sensors <b>106</b> and/or other sensing devices can sense pressure at preset intervals (e.g., once per minute) and only draw from the <figure-callout id="122" label="power source" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">power source</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b> at that time. Similarly, any diagnostics and/or forced flows (e.g., backflushing, described below) only occur periodically and thus only require power occasionally. In selected embodiments, the <figure-callout id="104" label="valve device" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">valve device</a></figure-callout> <b>104</b> only requires power when it changes position to adjust the pressure and/or flow rates. Without the need for any continuous substantial power, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> consumes much less power than would be required using a pump to drive body fluid. As described below, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can also include a hybrid mechanical and electrical device that reduces the required frequency of actuator movements, and thus further reduces power consumption. Accordingly, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can be configured such that the <figure-callout id="122" label="power source" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">power source</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b> runs the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> for extended periods of time (e.g., five or more years), and therefore does not necessitate frequent surgeries to replace the <figure-callout id="122" label="power source" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">power source</a></figure-callout> <b>122</b>.</div>
    <div id="p-0042" num="0041" class="description-paragraph">Optionally, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can also include a pump (e.g., an electro-osmotic pump) that can be activated to drive body fluid flow through the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b>. For example, the <figure-callout id="110" label="controller" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">controller</a></figure-callout> <b>110</b> can include logic that activates the pump when the orientation of the <figure-callout id="101" label="patient" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">patient</a></figure-callout> <b>101</b> is such that the body fluid flows in the reverse direction (i.e., retrograde flow) through the <figure-callout id="102" label="catheter" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">catheter</a></figure-callout> <b>102</b>. In other embodiments, the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> can include other suitable devices and features that facilitate the controlled drainage of body fluids.</div>
    <div id="p-0043" num="0042" class="description-paragraph">The subcutaneously installed <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> shown in <figref idrefs="DRAWINGS">FIG. 1A</figref> can also include features that limit the risk of infection during and after implantation. For example, components of the drainage system <b>100</b> (e.g., the <figure-callout id="102" label="catheter" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png,US09662478-20170530-D00002.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">catheter</a></figure-callout> <b>102</b>, the housing <b>128</b>) can include anti-fouling coatings and/or antibiotic impregnated materials. In selected embodiments, short-term thermal cooling and heating can be applied to the <figure-callout id="100" label="drainage system" filenames="US09662478-20170530-D00001.png" state="{{state}}"><a title="Show image containing callout" class="style-scope figure-callout">drainage system</a></figure-callout> <b>100</b> as a whole or components thereof to reduce bacterial colonization during the perioperative period.
